appraisal_events.evidence: guests who know they will never truly know "Oriane" strain to point her out to their wives: "Ursule, vite, vite, venez voir Madame de Guermantes qui cause avec ce jeune homme," as if at a public review.
appraisal_events.explanation: The crowd's eagerness to glimpse her, despite having no access to her circle, marks the duchesse as a figure of unreachable prestige.

appraisal_events.evidence: the narrator states her salon's preeminence exists only for those who read society columns rather than attend, "alors qu'il était un des derniers"; those who do attend come after imploring and rendering services, feeling they are doing her the honor.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator directly punctures the salon's outward prestige, showing it to be one of the least, not the most, elegant in Paris, sustained by print rather than genuine standing.

appraisal_events.evidence: left stranded among fashionable guests "comme deux hirondelles qui n'ont pas émigré à temps," she and her companion are not invited the following year, and when a cousin's intercession yields only a lukewarm reply, she withdraws.
appraisal_events.explanation: Once tolerated in the salon, she is quietly dropped and then declines the half-hearted invitation herself, a clear crossing from included to excluded.

appraisal_events.evidence: though rigidly antisemitic on principle, the prince receives Swann because he half-believes a legend, explicitly noted as false, that Swann's father was a natural son of the duc de Berri, making Swann in that fiction "n'avait rien que de chrétien."
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann is admitted as the sole exception to the prince's exclusionary circle, but only by way of a fabricated genealogy the narrator flags as untrue, so the inclusion is real yet founded on a discrediting premise about his actual origins.

status_effects.explanation: The crowd's visible straining to see her, though they will never know her, registers her as a figure of high, unreachable prestige.
The narrator's verdict strips away her salon's press-built reputation, exposing it as one of the least genuinely elegant.
Guests who attend do so feeling they confer an honor on her rather than receive one, a witnessed sign that her real standing is lower than her salon's public image.
She moves from marginal tolerance to being dropped from the guest list outright, and then withdraws after a half-hearted invitation.
Swann alone crosses into the prince's otherwise strictly exclusionary circle, though the boundary is bent for him only via a legend about his lineage rather than on his own account.

ambiguities: The passage names "la vieille Mme de Cambremer"; the reference sheet flags the surface form "marquise de Cambremer" as genuinely ambiguous between the marquis's wife (née Legrandin) and his mother, the dowager. The qualifier "vieille" (old) is read here as pointing to the dowager, la marquise douairière de Cambremer.
"le prince" is identified as prince de Guermantes only by inference from the earlier mention of the duchesse's cousin's household; his title does not appear explicitly in this passage.
